A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, proofs, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original graph-traversal and de novo molecule-generation experiments, including model ablations and generation-order analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original graph and molecule experiments and adds fragment-constrained generation results and further generation-order analyses.

M1.justification: LFlexMDM is renamed LoFlexMDM. The Kumaraswamy schedules, projected rate-matching objective, regularization, leave-one-out gradient estimator, backbone alternatives, and tau-leaping sampler are retained. Constrained generation evaluates existing checkpoints without introducing a new model component.

E1.justification: v2 adds four fragment-constrained molecular tasks: linker design, motif extension, scaffold decoration, and superstructure generation, using fragments from ten reference drugs. These introduce conditional completion requirements beyond v1's unconditional molecule generation. Star-graph coverage and SAFE training data are retained.

E2.justification: The corresponding graph and de novo experiments retain their comparator sets. The new constrained experiments extend comparison with SAFE-GPT/ARM, MDM, and FlexMDM; they do not introduce a distinct comparison method. Additional FlexMDM decoding configurations change settings rather than comparator identity.

E3.justification: The added constrained evaluation introduces fixed fragment-prefix completion, unchanged de novo checkpoints, 1024 sampling steps, and one completion per conditional input. v2 also adds unfiltered graph-order evaluation. Within retained experiments, the tabulated nucleus-sampling sweep drops p=0.2 and explicitly expands FlexMDM settings; the principal training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds molecular generation-time analysis across seven semantic token categories, supported by trajectories and Table 9. Appendix G.1.2 also tests whether graph-order conclusions survive removing the exact-match filter. Existing shared/separate-backbone and frozen/trainable-rate ablations remain.

E5.justification: v1 reports plus/minus values without specifying run counts. v2 identifies five de novo evaluation runs with different seeds and adds significance reporting for token-category timing, although the test is unspecified. Constrained-generation reporting is inconsistent: Table 3 says five runs, while Table 7 and Appendix F.2.4 say three. An increase in runs is not established.

E6.justification: De novo molecule scores are extensively revised: the medium-auxiliary, p=0.5, no-confidence row reports quality of 46.9% in v1 versus 79.5% in v2. The PDFs do not explain the broad score revisions, so these are reported replacements rather than established methodological gains. Constrained-generation and molecular-order results are added, while graph exact-match and token-accuracy scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 2 corrects the likelihood-bound statement from minimizing to maximizing a lower bound, and Section 3 corrects the worked drop-token projection example. The six propositions, their proofs, the terminal-KL bound, and the main schedule and gradient derivations are otherwise retained.

C1.justification: The central claim that learnable order dynamics improve insertion-based generation remains. v2 extends the claimed benefits to fragment-constrained generation, explicitly claims meaningful molecular ordering, and quantifies headline quality gains as 17.5 and 6.7 percentage points. The methodological contribution is not fundamentally redefined.

C2.justification: v2 adds a structure-before-chemistry interpretation of molecular ordering, a sharper explanation of schedule instability, and an explicit correlation-versus-causation qualification for graph analysis. Its new discussion addresses shared-backbone scaling, idle sampling steps, and SAFE representation redundancy. Appendix F.2.3 also explains the decision to omit FCD.

D1.justification: The sparse molecule setup in v1 is expanded into detailed dataset, decoding, and metric documentation. v2 specifies canonical-SMILES conversion, fragment and salt handling, deduplication, fingerprint diversity, QED/SA thresholds, and PyTDC components, and adds implementation-library and dataset access references. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously used processing.

R1.justification: The extended related work is substantially refocused: the learned-noise/image-diffusion discussion is removed, while insertion models, padding limitations, and learned generation order receive revised treatment. New references include Ding et al., the insertion-CTMC framework, Rainbow Padding, and molecular evaluation literature. v2 also explicitly positions the approach as applicable across three generation settings.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, related work moves after the experiments and new Discussion section, and the appendices gain a motivation section and reorganized experimental documentation. Model terminology is standardized around LoFlexMDM. These changes substantially alter the narrative beyond adding experimental content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with an explicit generator architecture panel. Graph displays are consolidated, and the retained loss plot is confined to the appendix. New constrained-result tables, molecular timing and trajectory figures, and filtered/unfiltered correlation panels substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by testing fragment-constrained transfer, checking graph-order conclusions beyond successful trajectories, and directly analyzing molecular ordering. Detailed metric documentation also addresses important reproducibility gaps in v1. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including inconsistent constrained-run counts and a headline 17.5-point comparison using FlexMDM quality of 62.0%, although Appendix Table 10 reports 63.2% under another decoding setting. The unexplained score revisions themselves do not establish improved paper quality.
